paras: The beating of "Abbidigal" was an attack in May 1888 in Green County, Georgia, in which Black followers of a self-styled "Holy One" pursued him after he left with their money, hanged him to a tree and lashed him until they believed him dead. He was found alive and cared for by white people, and the reports said he could not recover. Newspapers across the country carried the story chiefly because, they said, the "Holy One" was a white man who had stained his skin to pass as Black.

According to a dispatch from Atlanta, a man "of mysterious manner and appearance" had settled in Green County a few weeks earlier, called himself "Abbidigal" or "Holy One," and claimed a divine revelation instructing him to free Georgia's Black people "from the bondage of a false religion." He held services in fields and groves dressed in turbans and robes, drew listeners from neighboring counties, and sold beads and ornaments as shields against Satan. The Louisville Courier-Journal's version described him as a man of "olive complexion and black, bushy beard" who resembled an Egyptian. White residents, the dispatch said, regarded him as "a harmless crank" until he was found to be a thief and impostor.

He told his followers of a "land of promise" prepared for Black people, where they would neither work nor starve, and urged them to steal or sell what they had and give him the money before a departure on an appointed night. A dozen families sold their cabins, crops and other possessions and handed him the proceeds.

On the appointed night about forty men, women and children gathered at an isolated spot and waited in vain, while he was learned to be several miles away, heading across the country in the opposite direction. The dispatch placed this gathering "two nights ago," which falls around May 22 in the Courier-Journal's special dated May 24 and around May 23 in the versions dated May 25. Realizing they had been robbed, the followers pursued and caught him, hanged him to a tree, and lashed his naked body with brier reeds until they believed him dead, then left him.

White people later found him and cared for him; the Courier-Journal said that "Capt. Land, an officer of the law," found him an hour afterward and cut him down speechless, and that he lay "in a dying condition." The same version said several hundred dollars was found on his body. The dispatch added that he was a white man who had stained his face, hands and hair to pass as Black.

The reports said he could not recover, but no later report of his death, recovery or true identity appears in the coverage. No report of arrests, an inquest or other official action against his followers was found.

The story moved as a wire item, first appearing in the Washington Evening Star on May 25 under the headline "Lynched by His Dupes," with a Chicago dateline citing an Atlanta dispatch. Over the next two weeks it ran in papers including the Portland Daily Press, the New York Sun, the Wheeling Register, the Clarke Courier of Berryville, Virginia, the Bridgeton Pioneer and the Willimantic Journal, often in columns of miscellaneous news. Headlines went beyond the text: the Star's subhead had him "Switched to Death" and the Wheeling Register's said he was "Beaten To Death," though the reports beneath both said only that he would not recover.

Shorter rewrites changed the violence itself, with the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer saying he was "severely beaten," the Maysville Evening Bulletin that his dupes "nearly beat him to death," and the Kenosha Telegraph that they tied him to a tree and lashed him "until he was fatally injured," none of them mentioning a hanging. The Martinsburg Herald summed it up as "the lynching of a white imposter by infuriated colored people." Overall the papers presented the episode as a swindle and a curiosity, under headlines such as the Sun's "A Sacrilegious Fraud" and "Burnt Cork Abbidigal" and the Willimantic Journal's "Robbed by a Pretender," and the wire text cast the followers as credulous dupes of a "colored Saviour."

Accounts differed on the outcome: the dispatch's text said he was alive but could not recover or lay dying, while two headlines reported his death and the Kenosha Telegraph called him fatally injured. His assumed name was also printed as "Abidgal" and "Abbidgal." Every detailed version traces to a single Atlanta dispatch, and no Georgia local account confirming the details was found.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A swindler posing as a 'colored Saviour' took the money of a dozen families and fled; the deceived followers caught him, hanged him to a tree and lashed him until they thought him dead; white people found him; he cannot recover; he is a white man in disguise.

accounts.label: Short rewrites
accounts.gist: Briefs reduced the story to a beating: 'severely beaten', 'nearly beat him to death', or tied to a tree and lashed 'until he was fatally injured', with no hanging.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Atlanta dispatch as a curiosity under headlines such as 'Lynched by His Dupes', 'A Sacrilegious Fraud ... Burnt Cork Abbidigal' and 'Robbed by a Pretender', portraying the followers as credulous and the man as a thief.
The Martinsburg Herald called it 'a remarkable story' of 'the lynching of a white imposter by infuriated colored people'.
